pages.title: Gameplay
pages.blurb: How Familiar plays: the loop, encounters, collecting and battles.

items.n: The Pokémon loop is the heart: find characters, build a team, climb to Champion (and later the ranked PvP ladder). Test: does this make collecting or battling more fun? If it does neither, it is a side feature or a cut.
Full name: every clue is true, the conclusion is wrong. Bright, then dark, and built to read differently the second time. Test: does this plant something the player will reread later?
Characters are copies rebuilt into our world; merged cities and chaos zones follow logic you can explain. Test: does this have a reason inside the world? 'Because it's a game' gets questioned.

Battle depth players discover for themselves. Strong characters have gaps to exploit; weak characters have niches if you know how to use them, for mono and dual types. Test: does this create a new strategy or counter, or does it make one option simply better? Name picked 2026-10-20 over 'Every character has a use'.

items.t: Hard rule: no pay to win
items.n: Never. Power comes from skill and strategy, never from spending. Not a pillar: pillars guide choices, this one is never up for debate, and it governs monetization.
'Your journey, a shared world' was cut as a pillar. Shared world is a feature (kept in Vision); 'the story is about you' is covered by pillar 2.
Hidden wild encounters, trainer battles, collecting and building the best team.
The main goal. Side goals are the player's choice: strongest team, collect everyone, rare characters, side quests.
Keyboard and mouse first.
Your progress is personal. Other players are visible in the world.
Real anime characters, renamed and remodeled to stay recognisable. Alongside them: folklore, myths and a few non-anime picks.
Patches of distorted or space-textured ground on routes. Walking in can trigger an encounter.
You can see the zone but never who is in it, like tall grass.

Fire, Water, Ice, Wind, Earth, Lightning, Light, Dark, Spirit, Cosmic, Time, Tech, Beast, Blood, Neutral. Grass, Poison and Sound were left out (too few characters fit). Time and Cosmic are rare and powerful.
A character's type comes from what they fight with, not their anime's genre. Genre stays as flavor for city themes and zone looks.
Allowed when the character's traits support it (Naruto = Wind + Beast because of Kurama). Most final forms are dual. Gag reasons count (Patrick is Water/Earth because he lives under a rock).
A true neutral like Pokémon's Normal, for characters whose power is skill, strength or a quirk (Luffy, Nanami, Ayanokoji).
Joke picks are in on purpose, e.g. Inazuma Eleven players, Cole Palmer, Sunthorn Phu, the Bocchi the Rock band, SpongeBob and Patrick, Doraemon, Gold Ship, the Vergil chair.
Folklore, myths and other media join the anime cast: Nessie, Poseidon, Buddha, Cole Palmer, Sunthorn Phu, Baymax, Metro Man.
Roster characters tagged as villains are the ones the Unbound hunt. See Roster, Villains & gags.
There will be tiers. Details later.
Battles against other collectors, like Pokémon trainers.
Turn-based battles, like Pokémon.
One vs one by default. Two vs two is the most that ever fights at once, for special battles only.
Switching characters mid-battle is allowed.
Like Pokémon: super effective (double), resisted (half), immune (zero). Every type except Neutral has resistances.

Type balance is fairly strict. Many strategies must exist for players to discover: stat maxing, finding gaps in strong characters, niche uses for weaker ones, for both mono and dual types. No pay to win.
Planned later: areas where players battle each other and climb ranks. A feature under pillar 1, but it means balance must hold up against people, not just bosses, from the start.

A character uses moves of their own type(s) plus Neutral moves, and a few off-type moves only when the character has a real reason in their anime (e.g. Killua: a Dark move from assassin training; Luffy: a Fire move from Red Hawk). Coverage stays rare and lore-backed, and those off-type moves are hidden niches (pillar 4). Each off-type move needs a written justification.

Each character equips four moves picked from a pool they learn over time, plus one signature move that is unique to them and always equipped (e.g. Gojo's Hollow Purple, Luffy's Gear form). The signature keeps each character feeling like themselves; the four open slots are where builds and off-type surprises live. Signature moves must not decide fights alone.
Each move has a limited number of uses per battle, like Pokémon's PP. Strong moves are kept in check by countermeasures: fewer uses, recoil, and side effects.

No blanket rule. Whether a signature has a drawback depends on the character and other factors: a move that looks very strong on paper needs no drawback if the character's attack is low, because the whole character is what gets balanced.
Works like Pokémon. Each character has a fixed list of moves learned at set levels, plus TMs. No daycare and no breeding.

Characters evolve in 2 or 3 stages that follow their anime's arcs (Recruit, Hinokami, Sun Breathing Tanjiro). A character's type can change between stages: Tanjiro goes Water, then Water/Fire, then Fire.

pages.title: Lore
pages.blurb: How the world came to be like this, including what the player doesn't know yet.

items.n: Starts bright and adventurous. The story opens into dark turns as it goes.
The whole world doesn't realize what is really going on. The player does.
The story should have major twists and read differently after you finish it, like AOT.
A few years from now.
Someone built technology that re-imagines anime characters into the real world.
Using it also merged parts of the anime worlds with ours, changing the world map.

The one thing the game accepts: the Maker's tech rebuilds characters from everything that exists about them (episodes, art, scripts, fan data) and makes them physical. No real anime worlds. This is also why folklore and myth characters can exist: centuries of data.
Re-imagined rebuilds, not the originals, so many copies of the same character can exist, each slightly different.
A character doesn't make sense without their world, so to keep an unanchored copy stable the system renders pieces of their world around them. That is the merge and the anime cities.
A contract gives a character a place in our world, so the system stops rendering their home. Characters are partners, not prisoners.
The first company. Created re-imagined characters and the contract device that makes people trainers. Started as a worldwide trend: battles, collecting.
Like Pokémon Go: get the device and catch characters. People without a device can't see them. After the patches appear, people start seeing them, and eventually everyone does and has to live with it.
Patches start appearing worldwide for reasons unknown. The world declares a code red: this is changing the world itself.
A second organization claims it stopped the patches but cannot reverse them. Some cities are permanently merged with anime cities.

The Shield says the 6 most affected cities each need a strong trainer to halt the merge, each a different type so powers don't overlap. The Elite Four and Champion maintain the whole world. Any title can be taken by a stronger challenger, and holders get big benefits.
Without it they stop being trainers and lose their characters and status.

The Shield re-releases the device to everyone as a way to help save the world and says it is harmless. You don't have to battle: just owning a character helps stabilize the world, even if it only does chores like a fire character lighting kindling. People are pushed into it and mostly believe it. It is literally true.
Breaking a contract or abandoning a character is illegal. Secretly: broken contracts become loose threads.

Every Master's arena sits on its city's biggest chaos zone, with a node underneath controlling that vent. All six link to a core at the League summit, keyed to the Champion. It can only be shut down by the Champion with a hidden shutdown key.
A node can only grab what is tearing it, and freezes it. Normal characters don't tear the render, so they can't be taken. Frozen villains become anchored to the node, so they add no pressure.
The Shield stopped new patches but can't reverse existing ones. Secretly, the existing zones are the vents.
Energy leaking from the vents forms copies on its own. Trainers catching them ties the loose threads down.
Anchoring only works through the strongest bond, so the strongest trainer must hold the seat. The Shield watches you and hopes you'll believe them by the top.
They try to tell you, or plan to after the ceremony. After the villains fall you don't believe them, and you act first.
A former Maker or Shield worker who saw half the truth and left. That's how they know villain power can break the system.
You only take the device to investigate and climb, believing you're adding to the problem. You were actually helping.

Held contracts are stable anchors. Anything unanchored builds pressure toward a total merge: broken or abandoned contracts, and wild copies forming in chaos zones. Catching a wild character ties down a loose thread. Battles strengthen bonds. Ripping off devices would snap millions of anchors loose at once, so the truth can't be told.
Former Maker scientists founded the Shield and opened the patches on purpose to let pressure out, sacrificing some cities. The League really does anchor the world.
Places where the rendering broke or overflowed. The space texture is the unfinished render. Secretly they are the Shield's vents.

pages.title: World
pages.blurb: Cities, routes and how they connect.

items.n: Each one is a real place merged with an anime world.
Routes connect the cities.
Brick Bronze-style gatehouses you walk through between sections. The whole world lives in one Roblox place.

pages.title: Glossary
pages.blurb: The words Familiar uses, and what they mean.

items.n: The Maker's device and the game's title. In folklore a familiar is a spirit companion bound by a pact; it also means something you recognise. At the end you become someone's familiar. Picked over Recast, Revenant, Rendrant and others.
The characters you link. Brand and creature share the name, like Pokémon.
Trainers. Friendly, and quietly the job the system needs people to do.
The contract. You bind a familiar instead of catching it.
Wild copies with no Keeper: the loose threads.
Street slang for strays that turn dangerous. The Maker hates the word.
The chaos zones: where the world's fabric wears through. Walking in means you enter the fray. Ties to loose threads.
The Maker. Short and warm, from 'kith and kin'.
The Shield. A ward is a protective charm, and they really are protecting the world.
The six city Masters, who hold the wards over each node.
The Elite Four.
The villain group, who want to break bindings by force.

pages.title: Art & style
pages.blurb: The look, rig, animation and camera rules for anyone making assets.

items.n: Stylized anime units like Anime Vanguards or Anime Expedition: bigger heads, sculpted hair meshes, faces painted as textures.
Every humanoid familiar shares one R15 skeleton, chosen over R6 for now because bending elbows, knees and hands suit close-up cinematic moves.
For now: each fighting style gets its own version of the common moves, and every signature is fully custom. The prototype can start with one shared animation per move type.
Reusable scripted camera shots picked per move; custom keyframed camera only for signatures. Plan a skip or fast-animation setting.
Heavily cinematic, with lots of camera movement, mostly in battles. Animation Editor first, Moon Animator for cutscenes.

pages.title: Roadmap
pages.blurb: Where the project stands. Currently: pre-production.
pages.note: Items marked Plan are the working plan and may change.

items.n: Mostly done: pillars, hook, platform, target player. Gate: pillars agreed and the pitch fits in one sentence.

We are here. Living GDD, core systems on paper (moves, catching, stats, party size, rarity), a greybox battle prototype, a vertical slice (one city, route, Master), an art style target, a tech plan and a scope list. Gate: the slice is fun when other people play it. Done so far: names, moves, art target, roster database.
Content pipeline from data (roster, cities, story chapters). Alpha = every feature works. Beta = all launch content is in.
Balance, polish, bug fixing, closed playtests, launch, then updates. The post-game and ranked PvP fit as later updates.
Battle rules, character data and saving as tested code.
One city, one route with chaos zones, one Master. Greybox.
Other players visible, progress saved.
Add cities and routes from data.
Final look, then a public test and launch.
Built: this site holds every character, form, type, picture, villain and gag tag as data, editable online.
R builds this alone: code, models, animation, cutscenes, balance and planning. Every scope choice is weighed against that.
